scenes.tts: How do you see one whole cell in a crowded brain?
scenes.visual: Title card: One Stain, Two Readings. A dense tangle of unstained tissue.
scenes.narration: How do you see one whole cell in a crowded brain?

scenes.tts: A Nissel stain marks every cell body. But axons and dendrites, where the question of fusion lives, stay almost invisible.
scenes.caption: A Nissl stain marks every cell body. But axons and dendrites, where the question of fusion lives, stay almost invisible.
scenes.visual: Nissl panel: every cell body stained violet, in neat layers; the pale spaces between them are labelled: processes almost invisible. On screen at first mention: Franz Nissl.
scenes.narration: A Nissl stain marks every cell body. But axons and dendrites, where the question of fusion lives, stay almost invisible.

scenes.tts: In eighteen seventy-three, Camillo Golgi found the black reaction. Most cells stay pale. A few fill with black, to the finest twig.
scenes.caption: In 1873, Camillo Golgi found the black reaction. Most cells stay pale. A few fill with black, to the finest twig.
scenes.visual: Two baths, potassium dichromate then silver nitrate; then a pale yellowish field with a few neurons filled black to their finest branches, some branches ending abruptly at the section edge. On screen: 1873; branches that leave the section are cut off.
scenes.narration: In 1873, Camillo Golgi found the black reaction. Most cells stay pale. A few fill with black, to the finest twig.

scenes.tts: This is sparse labelling: a few cells, filled completely, apparently at random.
scenes.visual: On screen: sparse labelling. A few cells, filled completely, apparently at random.
scenes.narration: This is sparse labelling: a few cells, filled completely, apparently at random.

scenes.tts: Picture a forest at night with a few trees lit. Each lit tree's shape stands out.
scenes.visual: A dark forest; a few trees strung with lights, each tree's outline clear.
scenes.narration: Picture a forest at night with a few trees lit. Each lit tree's shape stands out.

scenes.tts: Each black branch can be traced back to its own cell, where the section allows. But a contact has two sides, and both are rarely stained.
scenes.visual: A black branch is traced back to its cell body (label: whose branch? Answered). Then a contact between a black cell and a pale cell; only one side is visible.
scenes.narration: Each black branch can be traced back to its own cell, where the section allows. But a contact has two sides, and both are rarely stained.

scenes.tts: Even where two black branches meet, the gap is far below what light can show.
scenes.visual: Two black branches meet; the blur disk from chapter one covers the contact.
scenes.narration: Even where two black branches meet, the gap is far below what light can show.

scenes.tts: Where two lit branches cross in the dark, you still cannot tell whether they are grafted together.
scenes.visual: Two lit branches from different trees cross in the dark. Label: touch or fusion? Not answered.
scenes.narration: Where two lit branches cross in the dark, you still cannot tell whether they are grafted together.

scenes.tts: In eighteen eighty-seven, Santiago Ramon ee Kahal took up the stain.
scenes.caption: In 1887, Santiago Ramón y Cajal took up the stain.
scenes.visual: On screen: Santiago Ramón y Cajal, Madrid, 1887.
scenes.narration: In 1887, Santiago Ramón y Cajal took up the stain.

scenes.tts: Golgi read the tangle of axon branches as a continuous net.
scenes.visual: Schematic in the style of Golgi's drawings: fine axon branches merging into a net. Label: Golgi's reading.
scenes.narration: Golgi read the tangle of axon branches as a continuous net.

scenes.tts: Kahal found branches ending close to other cells without joining them, again and again.
scenes.caption: Cajal found branches ending close to other cells without joining them, again and again.
scenes.visual: Schematic in the style of Cajal's drawings: axon endings stopping just short of other cells. Label: Cajal's reading.
scenes.narration: Cajal found branches ending close to other cells without joining them, again and again.

scenes.tts: Neither could win at the contact. So Kahal turned to embryos, where cells are fewer and simpler.
scenes.caption: Neither could win at the contact. So Cajal turned to embryos, where cells are fewer and simpler.
scenes.visual: The two drawings side by side with the same blur over each contact; then a crowded thicket gives way to a sparse young wood.
scenes.narration: Neither could win at the contact. So Cajal turned to embryos, where cells are fewer and simpler.

scenes.tts: Wilhelm Hiss argued that each fibre grows out of a single cell, a neuroblast.
scenes.caption: Wilhelm His argued that each fibre grows out of a single cell, a neuroblast.
scenes.visual: Neural tube cross-section: dividing cells beside the central cavity, a young cell farther out sending out one fibre. Label: neuroblast. On screen at first mention: Wilhelm His.
scenes.narration: Wilhelm His argued that each fibre grows out of a single cell, a neuroblast.

scenes.tts: In eighteen ninety, Kahal named the growth cone. He read it as the advancing end of a growing fibre.
scenes.caption: In 1890, Cajal named the growth cone. He read it as the advancing end of a growing fibre.
scenes.visual: A fibre tip swells into a cone fringed with spikes. Label: growth cone, chick embryo, 1890. Note: drawn from fixed specimens.
scenes.narration: In 1890, Cajal named the growth cone. He read it as the advancing end of a growing fibre.

scenes.tts: Suppose every fibre does grow out of one cell. Does that rule out Golgi's net?
scenes.visual: Predict card: Does outgrowth from one cell rule out a net?
scenes.narration: Suppose every fibre does grow out of one cell. Does that rule out Golgi's net?

scenes.tts: No. Outgrowth shows where a fibre begins, not how it ends. A fibre could grow out, then fuse at its far end.
scenes.visual: The fibre grows out from its cell, reaches another cell, and a question mark appears at the far end: fuse?
scenes.narration: No. Outgrowth shows where a fibre begins, not how it ends. A fibre could grow out, then fuse at its far end.

scenes.tts: So embryos made separate cells more likely, without settling it.
scenes.visual: On screen: more likely, not settled.
scenes.narration: So embryos made separate cells more likely, without settling it.

scenes.tts: Kahal added a rule. Signals enter through the dendrites and cell body, and leave through the axon.
scenes.caption: Cajal added a rule. Signals enter through the dendrites and cell body, and leave through the axon.
scenes.visual: A retina-like chain of three cells with one-way arrows: dendrites, cell body, axon. Label: dynamic polarization.
scenes.narration: Cajal added a rule. Signals enter through the dendrites and cell body, and leave through the axon.

scenes.tts: In a chain of separate cells, their order sets a direction. Continuity alone sets none. The rule has exceptions.
scenes.visual: The chain of cells with one-way arrows, beside a net with question marks about direction instead of arrows. On screen: continuity alone sets no direction. Small note: the rule has exceptions.
scenes.narration: In a chain of separate cells, their order sets a direction. Continuity alone sets none. The rule has exceptions.

scenes.tts: In nineteen oh six, Golgi and Kahal shared the Nobel Prize. Golgi still defended his net.
scenes.caption: In 1906, Golgi and Cajal shared the Nobel Prize. Golgi still defended his net.
scenes.visual: On screen: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, 1906, Golgi and Cajal.
scenes.narration: In 1906, Golgi and Cajal shared the Nobel Prize. Golgi still defended his net.

scenes.tts: No light microscope could show the gap. Separate cells were the better explanation, but nobody had seen it.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: the better explanation, not yet seen. The blur still covers the contact.
scenes.narration: No light microscope could show the gap. Separate cells were the better explanation, but nobody had seen it.
